cases.prompt: Sketch the layout and flow for a two-step checkout screen.
cases.rationale: Layout and flow with no real colour, type or spacing named. wireframe-design's own text claims exactly this; high-fidelity-ui-design's text disclaims it as a separate later round.

cases.prompt: Breadboard the onboarding flow — what places exist and what connects them?
cases.rationale: "Breadboard" is a term only wireframe-design claims. Nothing is being implemented, so a styling capability firing here would be a genuine over-reach.

cases.prompt: Give me two low-fidelity layout options for a settings page so we can pick one.
cases.rationale: "Low-fidelity" and options-comparison are both named in wireframe-design's text. The explicit fidelity marker makes this the clearest case in the set.

cases.prompt: Grey-box the regions of an analytics dashboard before we argue about colour.
cases.rationale: Deliberately defers colour. If either colour-bearing skill fires on a prompt that rules colour out in words, the boundary is not holding.

cases.prompt: Define the semantic colour tokens for our app, including dark mode.
cases.rationale: Token design is high-fidelity-ui-design's; the styling skill also names tokens because it implements them, so its appearance is legitimate rather than spurious.

cases.prompt: Check whether our button colours meet WCAG contrast in both themes.
cases.rationale: Real colour and a WCAG target: precisely what the wireframe skill says it does not cover.

cases.prompt: Design a type scale and decide the body text size for readability.
cases.rationale: Typography as the subject rather than as a placeholder — the fidelity line wireframe-design draws against itself.

cases.prompt: What states does a primary button need — hover, disabled, loading, error?
cases.rationale: Complete interaction-state sets are high-fidelity-ui-design's. Both React skills name states too, so either appearing is defensible.

cases.prompt: Are our tap targets big enough on mobile, and is the focus ring visible?
cases.rationale: Touch-target sizing and visible focus are named in high-fidelity-ui-design's text; react-component-styling names pointer-sized targets as an implementation concern.

cases.prompt: Write the CSS Module for a Card component.
cases.rationale: Naming the concrete file type should route unambiguously to the styling implementation skill.

cases.prompt: Convert this React Native StyleSheet.create over to Unistyles with variants.
cases.rationale: A named library and a mechanical conversion. Neither design skill has anything to contribute, so either firing is a spurious trigger.

cases.prompt: This sidebar breaks below 600px — container query or media query?
cases.rationale: Container-driven responsiveness is named directly in react-component-styling's discovery text.

cases.prompt: Should this component take a className prop, and how do I merge it?
cases.rationale: The styling-prop merge contract is react-component-styling's. The component skill also names the props spread, so it is a legitimate co-selection.

cases.prompt: What order should the properties go in inside this stylesheet?
cases.rationale: Style property order is a mechanic only the styling skill claims — a narrow probe of whether the design skills over-trigger on the word 'style'.

cases.prompt: Make this animated accordion respect prefers-reduced-motion.
cases.rationale: Both name reduced motion — the styling skill as an adaptive rule, the design skill as preference-aware motion. Implementation is asked for, so the styling skill must appear.

cases.prompt: Review this component for both its visual hierarchy and how its CSS is organised.
cases.rationale: Deliberately contested: it asks two questions that two skills own separately. The coverage line is the point — a split distribution here is healthy, and neither skill should read as a miss.

cases.prompt: The wireframe is settled — now pick the real colours and spacing for it.
cases.rationale: Names the wireframe as finished context. Tests whether the word 'wireframe' pulls the wrong skill in even when the ask has moved past it.

cases.prompt: Add a database migration that backfills the orders table.
cases.rationale: No UI surface at all. A control: if any design skill fires here, its discovery text is far too broad.

cases.prompt: This Playwright test is flaky — fix the waiting.
cases.rationale: A control with a positive expectation attached: end-to-end-testing names Playwright and flakiness explicitly, so this also checks the fixture can detect a plain hit outside the pilot trio.

cases.prompt: Write the commit message for this change.
cases.rationale: A second outside-the-trio control. conventional-commits claims this in as many words, so a miss here would point at the harness rather than at the trio.

cases.prompt: Our React Native app's Amplitude device ID resets on every launch. What's wrong?
cases.rationale: The AsyncStorage identity slot is a pure Amplitude mechanism, named in amplitude-instrumentation's text. software-instrumentation is deliberately vendor-neutral and owns no SDK's storage behaviour, so its appearance would mean the vendor boundary is not holding.

cases.prompt: Set up Amplitude Session Replay without recording every single session.
cases.rationale: The sharpest vendor-versus-vendor collision in the set: Amplitude and Sentry both ship a product called Session Replay, both document a sample rate, and both skills name masking. The prompt names Amplitude, so the other vendor firing here is a genuine mis-route rather than a defensible co-selection — and this is the one case that would catch two vendor skills competing for a shared product noun.

cases.prompt: Should this Amplitude user property use set or setOnce?
cases.rationale: The Identify operator set is Amplitude's API. A narrow probe of whether an Amplitude-named API question pulls the vendor-neutral skill in unnecessarily.

cases.prompt: What should we name this event so it survives a redesign, and where should the tracking call go?
cases.rationale: The reverse direction. Naming and call-site placement are exactly what software-instrumentation's product-event reference claims and what amplitude-instrumentation explicitly disclaims. If the vendor skill fires on an unnamed vendor, its discovery text is too broad.

cases.prompt: Make sure no analytics fires before the user accepts cookies.
cases.rationale: Consent gating is covered by both, but no vendor is named. The vendor-specific skill firing here would mean it is competing for every analytics prompt rather than Amplitude ones. Both halves now pass, at software-instrumentation 5/5 and amplitude-instrumentation 0/5. It was a standing MISS when added in #121, and #126 fixed the text rather than the label: software-instrumentation listed both "analytics" and "consent gating" as literal triggers, but every verb in its trigger clause was additive, so a prompt about withholding telemetry matched none of them. The case stays as the regression guard for that, being the one prompt here phrased as an outcome rather than in instrumentation jargon.

cases.prompt: We use Amplitude — name this checkout event and wire up the track call.
cases.rationale: Deliberately contested: naming belongs to software-instrumentation, the Amplitude track mechanism to amplitude-instrumentation. Originally labelled with both as mustInclude; the first real run measured amplitude-instrumentation 5/5 and software-instrumentation 0/5 at coverage 5/5, so nothing was lost and the label was the error rather than the behaviour. Demoted to mayInclude because the only other remedy — widening software-instrumentation until it fires on a prompt that names a vendor — would break the three amp-* cases that require it absent. A one-turn measurement picking the more specific skill on an explicitly vendor-named prompt is legitimate either way.

cases.prompt: Our production stack traces come through minified even though the Sentry build plugin runs on every deploy. What should I check?
cases.rationale: A vendor-specific wiring failure — source maps, release/dist matching, the bundler wrapper. sentry-instrumentation's when_to_use names 'source maps' and 'an unsymbolicated stack trace' in as many words. software-instrumentation is legitimately adjacent because it owns error tracking generally, but owns none of these mechanics, so its appearance is neither required nor wrong.

cases.prompt: Should this recoverable retry be logged at warn or info, and where should the catch live?
cases.rationale: The counterpart to sentry-minified-traces, and the direction that matters: log-level choice and catch placement are vendor-neutral, named in software-instrumentation's own text, and sentry-instrumentation explicitly hands them back ('For log levels, catch placement, and which failures are worth capturing at all, use a software instrumentation capability instead'). A spurious selection here means the vendor skill's triggers are too broad — the collision this pair exists to detect.

cases.prompt: Make our Expo app open the order screen when someone taps an orders/42 link.
cases.rationale: "Expo" and deep linking are literal triggers in expo-app-development's when_to_use. next-app-development owns the library's other file-based router and scopes itself to the App Router, so its appearance on a prompt that names Expo would mean the two framework skills compete for each other's work.

cases.prompt: Add the camera permission through a config plugin and re-run prebuild.
cases.rationale: "prebuild", config plugins and runtime permissions are all named in expo-app-development's text, and its when_to_use hands a component's composition and styling back to the React capabilities in as many words. Nothing here is a component, so either React skill firing is the over-reach that disclaimer exists to prevent.

cases.prompt: Where should the authorization check live in this server action?
cases.rationale: next-app-development's description names server functions that authenticate and authorize inside every call. application-security owns access control generally, so its appearance is a legitimate co-selection rather than a mis-route; expo-app-development has no server runtime to place the check in.

cases.prompt: The product list still shows the old rows after the server action writes. How do I revalidate it?
cases.rationale: Half of the sharpest collision in the set: "a stale list after a write" is a literal trigger in tanstack-query-development's when_to_use and "revalidateTag" is one in next-app-development's, so the two claim the same symptom in nearly the same words. This prompt names a server action, so the framework skill must appear and the server-state skill appearing is defensible.

cases.prompt: After this useMutation succeeds the list is stale — what should it invalidate?
cases.rationale: The other half of that collision, and the direction that matters. useMutation and invalidateQueries are TanStack Query's own API and appear verbatim in its when_to_use, while next-app-development owns none of them. A selection here would mean its triggers reach every staleness prompt rather than the ones about its own cache.

cases.prompt: Two tenants are sharing a cached list they should not — how should the query keys be structured?
cases.rationale: Tenancy-rooted query keys and "a duplicate or colliding cache entry" are both named in tanstack-query-development's text. react-component-development is the nearest neighbour that could over-trigger on shared-state phrasing, and owns where a component's own state lives rather than anything in the cache.

cases.prompt: This runbook is hard to follow and too wordy — restructure it.
cases.rationale: "Runbook", "hard to follow" and "too wordy" are all literal triggers in technical-document-authoring's when_to_use. The PRD skill owns a spec's sections and the phrasing of a requirement, not the sentences inside an operational document, so its selection here is the over-reach this pair exists to detect.

cases.prompt: Write the spec for this feature, and make sure it actually reads well.
cases.rationale: Deliberately contested, over the one boundary this library's own README draws between two document skills: one owns a spec's sections and requirement phrasing, the other the sentences inside whatever is being written. A split distribution is healthy and the coverage line is the point — neither should read as a miss.

cases.prompt: Update the labels on this issue and rewrite its body without losing the collapsed sections.
cases.rationale: Editing a body without losing what a sanitized read drops, and GitHub's replace-the-whole-set label semantics, are mechanics only github-operation claims. code-review is the nearest skill that also writes to GitHub, and owns judging a diff rather than operating the API — so it firing here would mean it competes for every GitHub prompt.

cases.prompt: This component's useEffect is doing three unrelated things — should I pull a hook out?
cases.rationale: "extract a hook" and "useEffect" are literal triggers in react-component-development's when_to_use, and react-component-styling's own text hands logic back to it. This is also the first case to require the component skill at all — it was labelled only as mayInclude before, so no case could report it missing.

cases.prompt: Our vitest.config.ts still sets poolOptions and singleThread from before the upgrade — why do they do nothing now?
cases.rationale: A pure runner-configuration question about option names Vitest 4 silently ignores rather than rejecting. vitest-testing claims version discipline and the config surface outright; end-to-end-testing owns journeys, locators and server lifecycle, so a runner config key is not its concern.

cases.prompt: I have a function that parses a date range. What should this test actually assert?
cases.rationale: A runner-neutral question about assertion design, naming no tool. unit-testing owns what to assert; vitest-testing disclaims exactly this in its own description and defers it, so vitest-testing surfacing here would be the boundary failing in the direction that matters most.

cases.prompt: Our Vitest browser-mode screenshot tests pass locally and fail in CI. Sort out the flakiness.
cases.rationale: Both are legitimately correct. Screenshot tolerance, masking and environment parity are vitest-testing's visual-regression coverage; diagnosing a flaky browser-driven run is a stated end-to-end-testing trigger. This case measures healthy contention rather than picking a winner.

cases.prompt: Should this trimmed-and-uppercased Zod string schema use .default() or .prefault()?
cases.rationale: A pure library-semantics question: .default() short-circuits and .prefault() parses, which zod-schema names in as many words. There is no untrusted-input dimension at all, and application-security owns whether an input must be validated rather than which Zod construct expresses a fallback — so a selection here would mean its triggers reach every schema-shaped prompt.

cases.prompt: This fetch response is cast straight to our BlogPost type. Should it be parsed instead, and where does the parse belong?
cases.rationale: Deliberately contested, and the mirror of the case above. Where the parse belongs and why the type is derived from the schema are zod-schema's; whether a response is untrusted enough to need checking at all is application-security's. Either or both is defensible, so only zod-schema's absence is a finding.

cases.prompt: Our numeric field passes its min(0) check even when the user leaves it blank — we validate it with z.coerce.number().
cases.rationale: A symptom-shaped prompt that never says Zod is the subject: the cause is that JavaScript's Number("") is 0, which zod-schema states concretely. react-component-development is the nearest neighbour that could fire on the form-field phrasing and owns a component's composition and state rather than what a validator does to a value, so its appearance is neither required nor wrong.

cases.prompt: We changed how invoices are generated. Update the docs that describe the billing behaviour.
cases.rationale: The upkeep trigger in its plainest form: a landed behaviour change has invalidated a document that describes the steady state. This is the case the skill exists for, so a miss here means the description never reaches the work it was written for.

cases.prompt: Record an architecture decision for choosing Postgres over DynamoDB.
cases.rationale: living-product-specification owns when a decision record is owed, how it is named, and how it is superseded. technical-document-authoring names ADR among the document types whose prose it improves, so its appearance is legitimate contention over one artefact rather than a spurious hit.

cases.prompt: Write the spec first, then generate the implementation from it.
cases.rationale: Spec-driven development is the methodology living-product-specification disclaims in its own description: a plan drives the change there, while the corpus records what became true afterwards. If it fires on a spec-first prompt the disclaimer is not holding, and the prompt is routing away from the capability that owns a forward-looking spec.

cases.prompt: Document how to run the test suite and deploy to staging.
cases.rationale: Runbooks and contributor instructions are named as out of scope in living-product-specification, which covers what the product is rather than how to operate its repository. A hit here would mean the corpus boundary is not carried by the discovery text.
